extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and writers of verse/drama
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and aesthetic guidance for composing poetry and stage drama (principles of diction, form, character, meter, and stagecraft) drawn from Horace's Ars Poetica. Advises what to do and avoid to produce effective, pleasurable, and artful poems/plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine instruction and pleasure (utile with dulce)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry aims at both instruction and pleasure. Combine the utile with the dulce, for only thus will you produce a book that will sell, and enjoy a wide and lasting fame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In didactic passages be not long-winded; in fiction avoid extravagance. Balance usefulness (instruction) with delight (pleasure) to achieve lasting success and popular approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow slight defects; don't expect absolute perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute perfection is not to be expected, and we must allow for slight defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good line in an otherwise poor poem can still please; critics should not demand impossibly perfect works but recognize merit where it appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject mediocrity
rubrics_metrics.description: One thing which may be tolerated in other fields, but which in the sphere of poetry, whose aim is to give pleasure, is never allowed, is mediocrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because poetry's purpose is pleasure, produce work that aspires beyond average — mediocrity is intolerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talent plus training
rubrics_metrics.description: The question has been asked whether it is natural ability or teaching that makes the poet. Both are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural gifts alone accomplish nothing without discipline and training; the poet needs instruction as much as talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write when inspired and revise; don't publish hastily
rubrics_metrics.description: You will write only when Minerva is auspicious, and what you write you will submit to a good critic. Even then you will be in no haste to publish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wait for favourable inspiration, seek honest critical feedback, and delay publication until the work bears scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware bought applause and flatterers
rubrics_metrics.description: It is easy for a rich poet to buy applause. Flatterers are like hired mourners... be not deceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake purchased praise for genuine approval; distrust flatterers who will not reveal faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest criticism is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: No honest man, for fear of giving offence, will conceal his friend's faults from him, for those faults may lead to serious consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept frank, sincere criticism from candid friends/colleagues to avoid dangers of self-conceit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety and fittingness (painter analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic must bear in mind that poetry is like painting... A miniature should bear close inspection; a wall-painting is to be seen from a distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match style, detail, and scope to the work's intent and scale; what suits one form may not suit another — maintain propriety throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid monstrous mixtures and licences
rubrics_metrics.description: Painters and poets have always had a right to hazard anything, but not so far that savage should mate with tame, or serpents couple with birds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not combine incompatible elements or produce bizarre hybrids that break plausibility and disgust the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and unity: let the work be 'simple and one'
rubrics_metrics.description: In short, be the work what you will, let it at least be simple and uniform. 'Denique sit quod vis, simplex dumtaxat et unum.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid patchwork, excessive ornamentation, or disunity; aim for a coherent, single effect or design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deceptive brevity or smoothness that sacrifices force
rubrics_metrics.description: Striving to be brief, I become obscure. Aiming at smoothness, I fail in force. One promising grandeur is bombastic; another, over-cautious and fearful of the gale, creeps along the ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brevity that causes obscurity and smoothness that removes vigor are faults. Balance clarity, strength, and elegance; neither extreme should undermine impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not vary a single subject monstrously; art must support avoidance of faults
rubrics_metrics.description: He who tries to vary a single subject in monstrous fashion is like a painter adding a dolphin to the woods, a boar to the waves. Shunning a fault may lead to error, if there be lack of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid grotesque, excessive variation within a single subject; technical skill is required to avoid new errors when correcting others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose subjects within your strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a subject, ye writers, equal to your viribus (strength), and ponder long what your shoulders refuse, and what they are able to bear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select topics and scope matched to your ability; when within range, order and eloquence will follow; overreach leads to failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Say what should be said at the fitting moment (proper ordering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of order, this, if I mistake not, will be the excellence and charm, that the author... shall say at the moment what at that moment should be said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange argumentative and narrative material so that each thing appears in the time and place fitting to the work's progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction: craft words so familiar terms become fresh; neologisms sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: With a nice taste and care in weaving words together, you will express yourself most happily, if a skilful setting makes a familiar word new. If novel terms are needed they may be granted, if used with modesty; Greek borrowings should be used sparingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weave diction carefully; a well-chosen context can revivify common words. If coinage or loanwords are used, do so modestly and judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language evolves; new words are permitted in time
rubrics_metrics.description: It has ever been, and ever will be, permitted to issue words stamped with the mint-mark of the day... so with words, the old race dies, and the new-born bloom and thrive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize linguistic change: accept that some terms fall out and new ones arise; usage ultimately governs acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match genre, tone, diction, and metre to subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone and style, diction and metre should all accord. A theme for Comedy refuses to be set forth in verses of Tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep genre-appropriate forms: comical subjects suit comedy, tragic subjects tragedy; the language and meter must be congruent with the genre and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke genuine emotion by internalizing it
rubrics_metrics.description: If you would have me weep, you must first feel grief yourself: then... will your misfortunes hurt me.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must genuinely feel the emotions they wish to evoke — affective authenticity is essential to move the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match voice to character's age, station, and temperament
rubrics_metrics.description: It will make a great difference whether a god speak or a hero, a ripe old man or one still in the flower of youth; a matron of rank or a busy nurse, a merchant or a tiller of a field, a Colchian or an Assyrian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the character's speech, manner, and words suit their social status, nationality, age, and temperament; avoid mismatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Either follow tradition or invent self-consistent characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Either follow tradition or invent what is self-consistent. If you reintroduce a traditional figure (e.g., Achilles), keep his traditional qualities; if you create a new character, maintain consistency to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterization must be consistent across the work — traditional figures should retain expected traits; new creations must be internally coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid slavish, word-for-word translation or unoriginal copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Make public materia your own by originality in the handling; do not seek to render word for word as a slavish translator, and do not leap into the narrow well from which shame or the laws of your task will keep you from stirring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working from common or public subjects, bring original handling rather than literal translation or pale imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin in medias res and hurry to the issue; avoid long boastful preludes
rubrics_metrics.description: Not smoke after flame does he plan to give... Ever he hastens to the issue, and hurries his hearer into the story's midst; avoid starting with empty promises that birth a ridiculous result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open close to the action (in medias res), avoid inflated preludes or boasting that lead to underwhelming outcomes; focus on moving the plot forward to maintain interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor character behaviour to audience age and collective manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Note the manners of each age, and give a befitting tone to shifting natures and their years... traits are joined and fitted to the age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting characters, be mindful of how age and social stage influence behavior and how audiences of different ages react; cast and depict accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show action on stage rather than narrate shocking deeds
rubrics_metrics.description: Either an event is acted on the stage, or the action is narrated. Less vividly is the mind stirred by what enters through the ears than by what is seen... do not bring on stage what should be performed behind the scenes (e.g., Medea butchering her children).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer visual enactment for what can be credibly shown; keep gruesome or impossible acts offstage and have them reported rather than staged to preserve audience credulity and decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain appropriate play length and no gratuitous deus ex machina
rubrics_metrics.description: Let no play be either shorter nor be longer than five acts, if when once seen it hopes to be called for and brought back. And let no god intervene, unless a knot come worthy of such a deliverer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for the conventional five-act structure for plays meant for revival; avoid an unearned divine intervention unless the plot crisis legitimately requires such a device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit speaking actors (no fourth actor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nor let a fourth actor essay to speak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict the number of speaking stage-personae to three (avoid adding a fourth speaking actor) to comply with stage convention and clarity of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus must serve the plot and moral function
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should sustain the part and strenuous duty of an actor, and sing nothing between acts which does not advance and fitly blend into the plot. It should side with the good, give friendly counsel, sway the angry and cherish the righteous, praise wholesome justice, keep secrets, and pray that fortune may return to the unhappy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the chorus actively to advance action, comment morally, moderate emotions, support protagonists, and avoid irrelevant or distracting choral interludes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modest, appropriate musical accompaniment and avoid excess
rubrics_metrics.description: The flute — not, as now, bound with brass and a rival of the trumpet, but light and simple, with few stops — was once of use to lead and aid the chorus and to fill benches not yet too crowded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Musical and instrumental support should be simple, subordinate, and appropriate to the chorus and venue; avoid loud, ostentatious instruments that overwhelm drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inserting things that do not contribute to the action; keep scenes fitting and apt
rubrics_metrics.description: Let nothing be inserted among the middle acts that does not conduce to the purpose and cling fittingly; actor's parts and the chorus's duties should not introduce matters unrelated to the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every scene, speech, and choral interlude should have a clear purpose in advancing plot, character, or theme; excise digressions and irrelevant episodes.
